world.setting: Mount Pleasant, South Carolina — an affluent, segregated 1990s suburb with manicured lawns, carpool routes, and a historically Black community (Six Mile) just across the highway
world.register: domestic horror — the menace hides behind Southern gentility and HOA respectability

patricia.name: Patricia Campbell
patricia.role: protagonist — suburban housewife, book club founder, the one who sees the monster first
patricia.look: White woman in her late thirties, medium build, shoulder-length brown hair pinned back, wearing a floral print dress with an apron, tired eyes, 1990s suburban mother

james.name: James Harris
james.role: antagonist — the vampire, a charming Southern gentleman who feeds on the invisible
james.look: Tall, lean white man in his early forties, dark slicked-back hair, sharp jaw, immaculate navy blazer over a crisp white shirt, unsettlingly polished smile, 1990s real estate investor look

carter.name: Carter Campbell
carter.role: Patricia's husband — ambitious psychiatrist, sides with James over his own wife
carter.look: White man in his early forties, tall athletic build, neat sandy-brown hair parted to the side, wire-rimmed glasses, wearing a button-down shirt with rolled sleeves, doctor's confidence

mrs-green.name: Mrs. Green

objects.why: Mount Pleasant homes — the domestic prison the women maintain and the vampire infiltrates
Rifle Range Road / the highway that separates white Mount Pleasant from Black Six Mile — geography as moral architecture
Southern gentility as protective armor — the social contract that shields predators
The family unit the women serve endlessly — carpools, casseroles, mother-in-law care
James Harris's charming facade; the women's polite Southern facade hiding their true-crime knowledge
The invisible labor that binds these women — domestic servitude disguised as love
Municipal police who won't investigate Six Mile; the legal system that protects the affluent
Carter's psychiatric credentials weaponized against Patricia; the threat of institutionalization
Missing children of Six Mile — deaths no one investigates
The true-crime paperbacks the book club reads — their subversive training manual for seeing predators
The women's growing investigative attention — Patricia building a case against James
Carter literally inviting the vampire in, using his authority as husband to crush Patricia's resistance

signatureObjects.name: Casserole Dish
signatureObjects.why: The casserole is the book's central symbol of invisible domestic labor — it's what Patricia delivers endlessly, what the neighborhood runs on, and ultimately the logistics network the women weaponize against the vampire. No shared icon depicts a baking dish.

signatureObjects.name: True-Crime Paperback
signatureObjects.why: The trashy true-crime books are the book club's subversive training — they teach the women to recognize predator patterns that James Harris embodies. The 'book' icon is too generic; this needs a blood-splattered pulp cover.

signatureObjects.name: Snake
signatureObjects.why: Patricia beats a snake to death with a rake in the garage bathroom — the book's first literal monster, foreshadowing the real one. Also: James as the serpent invited into paradise. No shared icon depicts a snake.

spine.claim: Patricia's daily life is already a horror movie — the invisible labor of carpools, casseroles, and senile mother-in-law care drains her before any vampire arrives.
James Harris doesn't break Mount Pleasant's rules — he exploits the infrastructure the suburb already built: racial invisibility, male authority, and women's silence.
When Patricia sees the truth, her own husband weaponizes his credentials to silence her — the social contract that was supposed to protect the family protects the predator instead.
Mrs. Green names the cowardice aloud — the white women protected themselves but never the children of Six Mile — and the book confronts its own racial blind spot.
The casserole network, carpool logistics, and gossip channels the suburb never valued become the tactical infrastructure that kills the predator.
